name: Livestock Health and Management
objectives: During a daily check of your animals, identify the signs of a healthy and a sick animal and separate one that may be sick, naming at least five warning signs and contacting the vet or animal health officer

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Signs of a healthy and a sick animal
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Do a quick daily health check and spot an animal that may be sick.
This lesson builds toward: During a daily check of your animals, you will identify the signs of a healthy and a sick animal and separate one that may be sick, naming at least five warning signs and contacting the vet or animal health officer.
You know your animals best. A daily look, at feeding or milking time, catches sickness early, when it is cheapest to treat and before it spreads.
A healthy animal is alert and curious, stands and walks normally, eats and drinks well, and cattle, goats and sheep chew the cud when resting. Eyes are bright and clear, the nose is clean, the coat or feathers are smooth and shiny, breathing is calm, and dung and urine look normal. A healthy hen is active, has a bright red comb, and lays as usual.
Warning signs: standing apart from the group, head down, not eating or not chewing the cud, dull or runny eyes, a runny nose, coughing or fast breathing, diarrhoea or blood in dung, limping, swellings, wounds, a sudden drop in milk or eggs, ruffled feathers, twisted necks in birds, or sudden deaths. Separate a sick animal from the others and contact your vet or animal health officer.
Step by step:
- Check every animal once a day, at feeding or milking time.
- Look: alert, standing and walking normally, eating, chewing the cud.
- Look closer: eyes, nose, coat or feathers, breathing, dung.
- Note any drop in milk or eggs.
- Separate any animal with warning signs.
- Write what you saw and call your vet or animal health officer.
Words to know:
- Chewing the cud: when cattle, goats and sheep bring food back up and chew it again; a sign of good health.
- Isolate: keep a sick animal apart from the others.
- Animal health officer: a trained government or private worker who helps farmers with animal health.
Try it now: Tomorrow at feeding time, check every animal with the list: alert, eating, chewing cud, eyes, nose, coat, breathing, dung. Write one line per animal (or per pen for poultry). Mark any you would watch or call the vet about.
You can now do a daily health check and spot the signs of a sick animal.

check.q: Which sign is a warning in a chicken?
check.why: Ruffled feathers are a warning sign; a healthy hen is active with a bright red comb.

check.q: You are busy and plan to check your animals only once a week. What is the risk?
options: Sickness is caught late, when it costs more to treat and may have spread
check.why: A daily look catches sickness early, when it is cheapest to treat and before it spreads.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Feed and water
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan feed and clean water for your animals through the year, including the dry season.
This lesson builds toward: For your animals through the year, you will plan feed and clean water, including the dry season, with no mouldy feed and feed changes made slowly.
Water comes first. Animals need clean water every day, and more in hot weather; a milking cow drinks a lot more than a dry one, and milk yield falls quickly without enough water. Keep troughs and drinkers clean and in the shade, and never let birds drink dirty, standing water.
Cattle, goats and sheep need roughage (grass, fodder such as Napier grass, Rhodes grass, desmodium or lucerne, and crop residues such as maize stover and bean haulms), plus energy and protein for animals that are milking, pregnant or growing. Goats also browse shrubs and tree leaves. Give mineral licks or salt as your vet or extension officer advises. Chickens kept for eggs or meat need a balanced feed; village chickens scavenge but lay and grow better with some extra grain, greens and clean water.
Plan for the dry season: grow fodder, and keep hay, silage or dried crop residues when there is plenty. Never feed mouldy feed: mould can carry aflatoxin, which harms animals and passes into milk and eggs. Change feeds slowly over several days to avoid stomach upsets.
Step by step:
- Give clean water every day; more in hot weather and for milking animals.
- Clean troughs and drinkers; keep them in shade.
- Plan roughage: pasture, fodder and crop residues.
- Add energy and protein for milking, pregnant and growing animals.
- Store hay, silage or residues for the dry season.
- Throw away mouldy feed; change feeds slowly.
Words to know:
- Roughage: bulky feed such as grass, hay and crop residues.
- Fodder: crops grown to feed animals, such as Napier grass or lucerne.
- Silage: green fodder stored airtight so it keeps for months.
- Mineral lick: a block of salt and minerals animals lick.
Try it now: List the feeds your animals get now and where each comes from. Mark which run out in the dry season and write one way to store or grow more before then. Check every drinker today and clean any that are dirty.
You can now plan feed and clean water for your animals through the year.

check.q: Which of these is roughage for cattle?
check.why: Roughage includes grass, fodder and crop residues such as maize stover and bean haulms.

check.q: On a hot day, your milking cow's trough is empty and dirty. What do you do?
options: Give her more dry feed instead
Clean it and fill it with clean water, in the shade
Let her drink from a standing puddle
check.why: Animals need clean water every day, more in hot weather, and milk falls quickly without it.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Housing and hygiene
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check your animal housing and set three hygiene rules for your farm.
This lesson builds toward: For your animal housing, you will check the housing and set hygiene rules for the farm, with dry, shaded, uncrowded housing, new animals kept apart and sick animals separated.
Good housing keeps animals dry, shaded, safe from thieves and predators, and not crowded. It needs fresh air without cold draughts, a dry floor that drains, and enough space for every animal to lie down, eat and drink. Crowded, damp, dirty housing spreads disease, worms and foot problems.
Keep it clean: remove dung and wet bedding often (it makes good compost), clean feeders and drinkers, and control flies, rats and wild birds. For poultry, use dry litter and replace it when wet. Wash hands after handling animals, especially sick ones.
Keep disease out and in: keep new animals apart from your herd or flock for a period your vet advises before mixing them, and keep sick animals in a separate pen. Some animal diseases also infect people, such as brucellosis and anthrax. If an animal dies suddenly with blood from the nose or other openings, do not open the carcass; keep people and animals away and call the vet at once. Dispose of dead animals the way your vet or animal health officer says.
Step by step:
- Check housing: dry, shaded, airy, drained, not crowded.
- Remove dung and wet bedding often.
- Clean feeders and drinkers; control flies and rats.
- Keep new animals apart before mixing, as your vet advises.
- Keep a separate pen for sick animals.
- Wash hands after handling animals; call the vet about sudden deaths.
Words to know:
- Litter: dry bedding such as wood shavings on a poultry house floor.
- Quarantine: keeping new or sick animals apart to stop disease spreading.
- Zoonosis: a disease that can pass between animals and people.
- Carcass: the body of a dead animal.
Official sources:
- FAO: Good biosecurity practices in small scale commercial and scavenging poultry production systems in Kenya
Try it now: Walk through your animal house or pen with the checklist: dry, shaded, airy, drained, not crowded, clean drinkers. Write one thing to fix this week, and three hygiene rules for everyone who works with your animals.
You can now check housing and keep it clean, keep sick and new animals apart, and act safely on a sudden death.

check.q: Why remove dung and wet bedding often?
options: Dirty, damp housing spreads disease, worms and foot problems
check.why: Crowded, damp, dirty housing spreads disease, worms and foot problems.

check.q: Rain leaked into your chicken house and the litter is wet. What do you do?
options: Replace the wet litter with dry litter and fix the leak
Leave it to dry by itself
Add feed on top of it
Move the birds into the rain
check.why: Poultry need dry litter; wet litter is replaced and the cause fixed.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Vaccination schedules with your local vet
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Agree a written vaccination schedule with a registered vet and keep vaccines working.
This lesson builds toward: With a registered vet or animal health officer, you will agree a written vaccination schedule and keep vaccines cool and in date, with each vaccine, the animals, the age and when to repeat.
Vaccines prevent many serious livestock diseases far more cheaply than treatment. Which vaccines your animals need, and when, depends on your country, your area and which diseases are present there. Common examples include foot-and-mouth disease, lumpy skin disease, anthrax and blackquarter in cattle; peste des petits ruminants (PPR) in goats and sheep; and Newcastle disease, Gumboro and fowl pox in poultry. Only a vet or animal health officer who knows your area can give the right schedule.
Ask your vet to write a year calendar: each vaccine, for which animals, at what age, and when to repeat. Use a registered veterinarian or a trained animal health worker. In Nigeria, the Veterinary Council of Nigeria keeps the register of veterinary surgeons; in Kenya, the Kenya Veterinary Board registers vets and para-vets; in Ghana, the Veterinary Services Directorate of the Ministry of Food and Agriculture runs animal health services and vaccination campaigns. Government campaigns are sometimes free or low-cost, so watch for announcements.
Vaccines are living or delicate products. Buy only from licensed agrovets, check the expiry date, keep them cool (in a cool box or fridge, out of the sun) from the shop to the animal, and use them as the label and the vet say. A vaccine that got hot may not protect your animals.
Step by step:
- Ask a registered vet or animal health officer which diseases are a risk in your area.
- Get a written year calendar: vaccine, animals, age, repeat dates.
- Buy vaccines only from licensed agrovets; check expiry dates.
- Keep vaccines cool from shop to animal.
- Use them exactly as the label and the vet say.
- Record each vaccination: date, animals, vaccine, batch, who gave it.
Words to know:
- Vaccine: a product that teaches an animal's body to fight a disease before it gets sick.
- Vaccination schedule: a calendar of which vaccines to give, to which animals, and when.
- Cold chain: keeping vaccines cool all the way from the maker to the animal.
- PPR: peste des petits ruminants, a deadly virus disease of goats and sheep.
Official sources:
- Veterinary Council of Nigeria (register of veterinary surgeons)
Try it now: Call or visit your local vet or animal health officer and ask: which diseases should I vaccinate my animals against here, and when? Write their answer as a 12-month calendar and save the vet's number in your phone.
You can now get a vaccination schedule from a registered vet and keep vaccines cool and effective.

check.q: Which is a vaccine-preventable disease of poultry?
check.why: Newcastle disease, Gumboro and fowl pox are common poultry diseases prevented by vaccines.

check.q: Your vet gave the first vaccines but nothing in writing. What do you ask for?
options: A vaccine for every disease in the world
A written year calendar: each vaccine, which animals, at what age and when to repeat
check.why: A written calendar from the vet keeps every vaccination on time.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Poultry biosecurity and Newcastle disease
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set biosecurity rules that keep Newcastle disease and other infections out of your flock.
This lesson builds toward: For a poultry flock, you will set biosecurity rules and an outbreak plan for Newcastle disease, with vaccination on the vet's schedule and the steps to take if birds die suddenly.
Newcastle disease is one of the most serious poultry diseases in Africa. The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) describes signs such as gasping, coughing and sneezing; nervous signs such as tremors, paralysis and twisted necks; diarrhoea; and a drop in eggs. Deaths can reach 100 percent of a flock, and almost all birds in a flock can be infected within a few days.
WOAH explains it spreads through contact with sick birds and their droppings, and on contaminated feed, water, equipment and clothing. That is why biosecurity, the simple everyday steps that keep germs out, matters as much as vaccination. FAO's guidance for small-scale flocks in Kenya stresses that many of these steps cost little or nothing.
Vaccinate the whole flock against Newcastle disease on the schedule your vet gives. For village chickens, FAO describes heat-tolerant vaccines (such as I-2) that can be given by eye drop; ask your animal health officer what is available. If many birds sicken or die suddenly, keep the flock shut in, tell the vet or animal health officer at once, and do not sell or move birds. WOAH advises leaving a cleaned house empty of poultry for 21 days before restocking after an outbreak.
Step by step:
- Keep visitors out of the poultry house; wash hands and use a foot dip or separate shoes.
- Buy birds only from trusted, healthy sources; keep new birds apart first.
- Keep wild birds, rats and other people's poultry away from feed and water.
- Clean and disinfect drinkers, feeders and crates often.
- Vaccinate the whole flock on the vet's schedule.
- If birds sicken or die suddenly: shut the flock in, call the vet, do not sell or move birds.
Words to know:
- Biosecurity: simple everyday steps that keep germs out of a farm and stop them spreading.
- Newcastle disease: a fast-spreading virus disease of poultry that can kill a whole flock.
- Foot dip: a tray of disinfectant people step in before entering an animal house.
- Thermostable vaccine: a vaccine that copes better with heat, useful in villages; it still needs to be kept as cool as possible.
Official sources:
- World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH): Newcastle disease
- FAO: Newcastle disease in village chickens
- FAO: Good biosecurity practices in small scale commercial and scavenging poultry production systems in Kenya
Try it now: Write five biosecurity rules for your poultry and post them at the poultry house door. Then ask your vet or animal health officer when your flock should next be vaccinated against Newcastle disease and add it to your calendar.
You can now protect a flock from Newcastle disease with biosecurity and vaccination, and act fast if birds die.

options: The simple everyday steps that keep germs out of a farm
check.why: Biosecurity is the everyday steps that keep germs out, and many cost little or nothing.

check.q: A neighbour whose birds have been sick wants to borrow your egg trays and feeders. What do you do?
options: Lend them and use them again when they come back
Do not share equipment, because germs spread on it
Lend them only for one day
check.why: Newcastle disease spreads on contaminated feed, water, equipment and clothing.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Parasites, records and when to call the vet
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan parasite control with your vet, keep a treatment record, and know the signs that need a vet at once.
This lesson builds toward: For your herd or flock, you will plan parasite control with your vet, keep a treatment record and list the signs that need a vet at once, recording every treatment with its withdrawal period.
Worms inside the gut and ticks, mites and fleas outside take blood, slow growth and spread disease; ticks spread East Coast fever in cattle in East Africa. Signs of worms include poor growth, rough coat, pot belly, diarrhoea and pale eyelids or gums. Reduce parasites with clean, dry housing, moving grazing animals to fresh pasture, and not overcrowding. Your vet can tell you when to deworm, dip or spray, and with which product. Always use the dose on the label or from the vet: too little lets worms and ticks become resistant, and too much can harm the animal.
Medicines leave residues. Every drug has a withdrawal period: the time after treatment before milk, eggs or meat from that animal can be sold or eaten. FAO stresses working with your vet on a health plan and recording each treatment with its withdrawal period. Never use antibiotics to make animals grow faster or without a vet's advice.
Records turn guessing into knowing. For each animal or flock, write: identity, births, vaccinations, treatments (date, product, who gave it, when the withdrawal period ends), weights or production, and deaths. A notebook works; so does a phone spreadsheet. Call the vet at once for: sudden deaths, several animals sick at the same time, an animal not eating for more than a day, difficult birth, heavy bleeding, nervous signs, or any disease your government says must be reported.
Step by step:
- Ask your vet for a parasite plan: when to deworm and dip or spray, and with what.
- Use the dose on the label or from the vet, never a guess.
- Move grazing animals to fresh pasture; keep housing dry.
- Record every treatment with the date the withdrawal period ends.
- Do not sell milk, eggs or meat before the withdrawal period ends.
- Call the vet at once for sudden deaths, several sick, difficult birth or nervous signs.
Words to know:
- Parasite: a worm, tick, mite or flea that lives on or in an animal and harms it.
- Deworming: giving a medicine to kill worms inside an animal.
- Withdrawal period: the time after a treatment before milk, eggs or meat can be sold or eaten.
- Resistance: when worms, ticks or germs survive a medicine that used to kill them.
Official sources:
- FAO: Prudent and efficient use of antimicrobials in pigs and poultry (vets, health plans, withdrawal periods)
- World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH): Newcastle disease
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page health plan. Include your daily check, feed and water plan, housing rules, the vaccination calendar from your vet, biosecurity rules, parasite plan, the records you will keep, and the signs that mean you call the vet, with the vet's name and number at the top.
You can now control parasites with your vet, keep treatment records with withdrawal periods, and know when to call the vet.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Daily check No daily check, or no warning signs listed. A daily check at feeding or milking time with the main warning signs and what to do. Fits the check to each kind of animal kept. Feed, water and housing No dry-season plan, or housing and hygiene rules missing. Feed and clean water through the year with a dry-season plan, and two housing and hygiene rules. Includes growing or storing fodder and keeping new animals apart. Vaccination schedule No schedule, or one not agreed with a vet. A written schedule from a registered vet, with how vaccines are kept cool and in date. Notes government campaigns and the vet's name and number. Biosecurity No biosecurity rules. Biosecurity rules, and for poultry, Newcastle vaccination and the steps if birds die suddenly. Low-cost steps such as hand washing and a foot dip are in place. Parasites, records and the vet No records, or doses guessed. Parasite control planned with the vet, a treatment record with withdrawal periods, and the signs that mean call the vet at once. Records also cover births, weights or production and deaths. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

check.q: Which disease do ticks spread in cattle in East Africa?
check.why: Ticks spread East Coast fever in cattle in East Africa.

check.q: You treated a goat today. What do you write in the record?
options: Nothing, if the goat looks better
Only the price of the medicine
The date, product, who gave it and when the withdrawal period ends
check.why: Recording each treatment with its withdrawal period keeps milk and meat safe to sell and eat.
